claim: Mammalian mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a double-stranded closed circular molecule of about 16 kb coding for 37 genes.
source: Mammalian mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a double-stranded closed circular molecule of about 16 kb coding for 37 genes.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about mitochondrial DNA supported by scientific consensus.

claim: The '9 bp deletion' (8271–8281) is seen in the intergenic region of cytochrome c oxidase II/tRNALys and is the most common mitochondrial deletion.
source: '9 bp deletion' (8271–8281), seen in the intergenic region of cytochrome c oxidase II/tRNALys, is the most common mitochondrial deletion.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The '9 bp deletion' has been associated with several diseases like myopathy, dystonia, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: While it is associated with several diseases like myopathy, dystonia, and hepatocellular carcinoma, it has also been used as an evolutionary marker.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research on disease associations.

claim: The '9 bp deletion' has been used as an evolutionary marker.
source: While it is associated with several diseases like myopathy, dystonia, and hepatocellular carcinoma, it has also been used as an evolutionary marker.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Endonuclease G can induce breaks at sequences associated with '9 bp deletion' when present on a plasmid or in the mitochondrial genome.
source: In the current study, we show that Endonuclease G, a mitochondrial nuclease responsible for nonspecific cleavage of nuclear DNA during apoptosis, can induce breaks at sequences associated with '9 bp deletion' when it is present on a plasmid or in the mitochondrial genome.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Endonuclease G binds to G-quadruplex structures formed at the hotspot and induces DNA breaks.
source: Through a series of in vitro and intracellular studies, we show that Endonuclease G binds to G-quadruplex structures formed at the hotspot and induces DNA breaks.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: Endonuclease G has a novel role in generating mtDNA deletions that depends on the formation of G4 DNA within the mitochondrial genome.
source: Therefore, we uncover a new role for Endonuclease G in generating mtDNA deletions, which depends on the formation of G4 DNA within the mitochondrial genome.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: The mammalian mitochondrial genome encodes for 13 respiratory chain proteins, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs.
source: The mammalian mitochondrial genome encodes for 13 respiratory chain proteins, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs (Chen and Butow, 2005; Clayton, 1984; Holthöfer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA is more prone to DNA damage than nuclear DNA, leading to the accumulation of 50 times more mutations, including deletions.
source: Due to its vital role in oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial DNA is frequently exposed to reactive oxygen species (ROS) and is more prone to DNA damage than nuclear DNA, leading to the accumulation of 50 times more mutations, including deletions (Chen et al., 2011; Hudson et al., 1998; Michikawa et al., 1999; Pakendorf and Stoneking, 2005; Yakes and Van Houten, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mitochondrial mutations have been associated with ageing and several disease conditions like myopathies, dystonia, cancer.
source: Mitochondrial mutations have been associated with ageing and several disease conditions like myopathies, dystonia, cancer etc. (Chen et al., 2011; Taylor and Turnbull, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Large-scale deletions of 200–5000 bp in mitochondria were associated with the progression of breast, colorectal, renal, and gastric cancers.
source: Mitochondrial mutations, especially large-scale deletions of 200–5000 bp, were associated with the progression of breast, colorectal, renal, and gastric cancers (Bianchi et al., 2001; Carew and Huang, 2002; Modica-Napolitano et al., 2007; Penta et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The well-studied phenotypes of mtDNA deletions are Kearns-Sayre Syndrome (KSS), Pearson syndrome, and progressive external ophthalmoplegia (PEO).
source: The well-studied phenotypes of mtDNA deletions are Kearns-Sayre Syndrome (KSS), Pearson syndrome, and progressive external ophthalmoplegia (PEO; Marni, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The presence of alternate DNA structures like G-quadruplex, triplex, and cruciform structures in the mitochondrial genome has been reported along with their association with different mitochondrial diseases.
source: The presence of alternate DNA structures like G-quadruplex, triplex, and cruciform structures in the mitochondrial genome has been reported along with their association with different mitochondrial diseases (Bharti et al., 2014; Damas et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2014; Oliveira et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Breakpoint regions reported in PEO patients were in the proximity of G-quadruplex motifs.
source: Breakpoint regions reported in the case of PEO patients were in the proximity of G-quadruplex motifs, further suggesting the role of non-B DNA structures in mitochondrial disorders (Bharti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: G4 forming motifs were located adjacent to mitochondrial deletion breakpoints associated with KSS.
source: G4 forming motifs were also located adjacent to mitochondrial deletion breakpoints associated with KSS, a clinical subgroup of mitochondrial encephalomyopathies (Van Goethem et al., 2003; Zeviani et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A G4 ligand RHPS4 preferentially localises to mitochondria and affects mitochondrial genome content, transcription elongation, and respiratory function.
source: Further, a G4 ligand RHPS4 preferentially localises to mitochondria and affects mitochondrial genome content, transcription elongation, and respiratory function (Falabella et al., 2019a; Oliveira et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In vitro results suggested that a single-base mutation in mtDNA (mt10251) was sufficient to form G4 DNA.
source: Moreover, in vitro results suggested that a single-base mutation in mtDNA (mt10251) was sufficient to form G4 DNA (Chu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ATP-dependent G4 resolving helicase Pif1 could unfold non-B DNA structures and continue the synthesis by mitochondrial DNA polymerases, Pol γ and PrimPol.
source: Importantly, ATP-dependent G4 resolving helicase Pif1 could unfold non-B DNA structures and continue the synthesis by mitochondrial DNA polymerases, Pol γ and PrimPol (Butler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) 9 bp deletion is caused by loss of one copy of the 9 bp repeat sequence (CCCCCTCTA) in the intergenic region of cytochrome c oxidase II (COII)/tRNALys.
source: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) 9 bp deletion caused by loss of one copy of the 9 bp repeat sequence (CCCCCTCTA) in the intergenic region of cytochrome c oxidase II (COII)/tRNALys is one of the most common deletions in mitochondria (Redd et al., 1995; Thomas et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The 9 bp deletion has been associated with hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: It has been associated with various diseases, including hepatocellular carcinoma (Jin et al., 2012; Komandur et al., 2011; Krishnan and Turnbull, 2010; Zhuo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The 9 bp deletion is widely used as a phylogenetic marker to study evolutionary trends and migration of populations.
source: The 9 bp deletion is also widely used as a phylogenetic marker to study evolutionary trends and migration of populations (Soodyall et al., 1996; Yao et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: mt4977 eliminates mitochondrial sequences between 8470 and 13,447 bp, which include the removal of genes required for normal oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source: mt4977 eliminates mitochondrial sequences between 8470 and 13,447 bp, which include the removal of genes required for normal oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) (Lee et al., 1994; Yang et al., 1994; Yen et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The role of replication slippage and DSB repair has been shown to play a role in the generation of mtDNA4977 in mammalian cells.
source: Recently the role of replication slippage and DSB repair has been shown to play a role in the generation of mtDNA4977 in mammalian cells (Phillips et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The presence of a 13 bp direct repeat plays a major role in mt4977, as only one of the repeats was retained following joining, indicating the involvement of microhomology-mediated end joining.
source: Previous studies have shown that the presence of a 13 bp direct repeat plays a major role in mt4977, as only one of the repeats was retained following joining, indicating the involvement of microhomology-mediated end joining (Samuels et al., 2004; Srivastava and Moraes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When restriction endonucleases were used to introduce DSBs, there was the accumulation of deletions, which further implicates the imperfect repair and deletion in the mitochondrial genome.
source: When restriction endonucleases were used to introduce DSBs, there was the accumulation of deletions, which further implicates the imperfect repair and deletion in the mitochondrial genome (Srivastava and Moraes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A previous study suggested the existence of microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) in mitochondria, which operate in a microhomology-dependent manner.
source: A previous study from our laboratory suggested the existence of microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) in mitochondria, which operate in a microhomology-dependent manner, explaining the frequently seen deletions in mitochondrial DNA (Tadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Five classical G4 DNA motifs are present in the mitochondrial genome, which could fold into G4 DNA.
source: In silico studies along with biochemical analyses revealed that 5 classical G4 DNA motifs are present in the mitochondrial genome, which could fold into G4 DNA (Cer et al., 2013; Dahal et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The '9 bp deletion' (8271–8281) occurs next to one of the 5 G4 motifs with the coordinate position 8252–8295 (designated as mitochondrial Region I).
source: Since '9 bp deletion' (8271–8281) is the most frequent mitochondrial deletion and occurs next to one of the 5 G4 motifs with the coordinate position 8252–8295 (designated as mitochondrial Region I) (Figure 1A and B; Dahal et al., 2022), we have investigated the putative role of G4 DNA structure in DNA breakage and formation of the mtDNA deletions.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1A and B and a citation.

claim: The G-rich strand of mitochondrial Region I forms both intra and intermolecular G4 DNA structure in a KCl-dependent manner.
source: Faster mobility of the G-rich strand compared to its complementary C-rich strand suggested the formation of both intra and intermolecular G4 DNA structure in a KCl-dependent manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The formation of intramolecular G4 DNA was abrogated when G-stretches were mutated.
source: Importantly, the formation of intramolecular G4 DNA was abrogated when G-stretches were mutated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Circular dichroism studies revealed that the G-rich strand exhibited the characteristic of a parallel G-quadruplex DNA with absorption maxima of 260–270 nm and absorption minima of 240 nm.
source: Further, circular dichroism (CD) studies revealed that the spectra exhibited the characteristic of a parallel G-quadruplex DNA with absorption maxima of 260–270 nm and absorption minima of 240 nm as opposed to the C-rich strand, which showed the maxima similar to that of a typical single-stranded DNA (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The guanine residues from the G stretches of the mitochondrial Region I motif participate in G-quadruplex formation.
source: The results suggest that the guanine residues from the G stretches of the mitochondrial Region I motif participate in G-quadruplex formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the DMS protection assay results.

claim: Based on CD studies and gel shift assays, a parallel, intramolecular G-quadruplex structure was modelled for mitochondrial Region I.
source: Based on CD studies and gel shift assays, a parallel, intramolecular G-quadruplex structure was modelled (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and modeling shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The Region I of mitochondrial DNA can fold into an intramolecular G-quadruplex.
source: Thus, our study reinforces that the Region I of mitochondrial DNA can fold into an intramolecular G-quadruplex (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental results shown in Figures 1E and F.

claim: An inverted repeat sequence (coordinate positions 8295–8363), which could fold into a cruciform DNA, was present adjacent to the G4 motif in mitochondrial Region I.
source: Interestingly, an inverted repeat sequence (coordinate positions 8295–8363), which could fold into a cruciform DNA, was also present adjacent to the G4 motif.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Primer extension assay on pDI1 revealed multiple polymerase pause sites, and the intensity of the pauses increased with increasing concentrations of KCl.
source: Results revealed multiple polymerase pause sites, and the intensity of the pauses increased with increasing concentrations of KCl (25, 50 and 100 mM; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was significantly fewer sites and less pausing observed in the absence of KCl, indicating the absence of the formation of intramolecular G-quadruplex species.
source: Interestingly, there was significantly fewer sites and less pausing observed in the absence of KCl, indicating the absence of the formation of intramolecular G-quadruplex species in these cases (Figure 2C, lane 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and inference from the results.

claim: The observed polymerase pause was due to the formation of G4 DNA, but not cruciform DNA.
source: Considering that the formation of cruciform DNA occurs irrespective of the presence of KCl, these results also suggest that the observed pause was due to the formation of G4 DNA, but not cruciform DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the KCl-dependence of the pause sites.

claim: The observed polymerase pauses mapped to the G-quadruplex motif.
source: Besides, the observed polymerase pauses mapped to the G-quadruplex motif (Figure 2C, lanes 7–9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Abrogation of G4 DNA structure by mutation of G4 DNA motif (pDI2) resulted in the disappearance of the observed pause site.
source: Abrogation of G4 DNA structure by mutation of G4 DNA motif (pDI2) resulted in the disappearance of the observed pause site, further confirming the above results (Figure 2D, lanes 3, 4 and lane 6, 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The appearance of strong polymerase pause sites were dependent on K+, but not on other monovalent cations such as Li+ or Na+.
source: It was also observed that the appearance of strong polymerase pause sites were dependent on K+ (Figure 2E, lanes 4–5; F), but not on other monovalent cations such as Li+ (with no or little G-quadruplex stabilising properties) or Na+ (with limited stabilising properties) (Figure 2E, lanes 6–9; F) suggesting that the non-B DNA responsible for polymerase arrest was G4 DNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Sodium bisulphite modification assay on pDI1 showed that 38 out of 40 clones sequenced showed C to T conversion to varying extents in either top or bottom strands.
source: Of the 40 clones sequenced, 38 molecules showed C to T conversion to varying extents in either top or bottom strands (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The cytosines complementary to the G-quadruplex motif exhibited single-stranded nature in pDI1.
source: Interestingly, the cytosines complementary to the G-quadruplex motif exhibited single-stranded nature (Figure 3A), suggesting the formation of a G-quadruplex structure in the complementary G-rich strand.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and inference from the results.

claim: Approximately 15% of molecules showed continuous conversion at the region corresponding to the G4 motif in pDI1.
source: Importantly, ~15% of molecules showed continuous conversion at the region corresponding to the G4 motif.
evidence: This is based on analysis of bisulphite sequencing data.

claim: Region I of mitochondrial DNA can fold into a non-B DNA even when cloned into a plasmid.
source: These results suggest that Region I of mitochondrial DNA can fold into a non-B DNA even when cloned into a plasmid, consistent with the result obtained following primer extension.
evidence: This is inferred from the bisulphite modification assay results.

claim: Bisulphite modification assay on mitochondrial DNA from Nalm6 cells showed that 52 out of 59 DNA molecules analysed showed C→T conversions to varying extents.
source: Results showed that out of 59 DNA molecules analysed following cloning and sequencing, 52 showed C→T conversions to varying extents (Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cumulative analysis of converted cytosines on a fragment of 281 bp revealed single-strandedness at Region I corresponding to the complementary region of G4 motifs in the mitochondrial genome.
source: Cumulative analysis of converted cytosines on a fragment of 281 bp revealed single-strandedness at Region I corresponding to the complementary region of G4 motifs.
evidence: This is based on analysis of bisulphite sequencing data from mitochondrial DNA.

claim: Among the 50 clones from the top strand of mitochondrial DNA, 14 (28%) had continuous conversions of 11 or more cytosines when a stretch of 20 cytosines modifications was considered on a single DNA molecule level.
source: Further, among the 50 clones from the top strand, 14 (28%) had continuous conversions of 11 or more cytosines when a stretch of 20 cytosines modifications was considered on a single DNA molecule level (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The formation of G4 DNA at Region I may not occur in all DNA molecules of the mitochondrial genome at a given time.
source: This suggests that the formation of G4 DNA at Region I may not occur in all DNA molecules of the mitochondrial genome at a given time.
evidence: This is inferred from the bisulphite sequencing data showing variable conversion rates.

claim: The G-quadruplex motif at Region I can fold into a G-quadruplex structure in mitochondria.
source: However, based on these results in conjunction with biochemical assays, it is evident that the G-quadruplex motif at Region I can indeed fold into a G-quadruplex structure in mitochondria.
evidence: This is based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: BG4 antibody can bind to G-quadruplexes formed in DNA and RNA.
source: The previous studies established that BG4 antibody can bind to G-quadruplexes formed in DNA and RNA (Chambers et al., 2015; Das et al., 2016; Javadekar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: BG4 localizes to mitochondria in HeLa and HEK 293T cells.
source: Merging of green and red foci resulting in yellow foci was observed in the case of both HeLa and HEK 293T cells, which revealed localisation of BG4 to mitochondria (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Colocalisation analyses show Mander's coefficient value between 0.25–0.4 for BG4 and MitoTracker in HeLa and 293T cells.
source: Colocalisation analyses show Mander's coefficient value between 0.25–0.4, irrespective of the stain used as MitoTracker, in the case of HeLa and 293T cells indicating that G-quadruplex structures can be detected in the mitochondrial genome in cellular context (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: In Rho(0) cells, BG4 foci do not colocalize with mitochondria.
source: Results suggested that although BG4 foci were observed in the cytoplasm of Rho(0) cells, they do not seem to colocalize with mitochondria (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: BG4 can bind to G-rich oligomer (G1) but not to C-rich oligomer (C1) in vitro.
source: Results indicated that the bound complex was seen when G-rich oligomer (G1) was incubated with BG4, while such binding was absent when incubated with C-rich oligomer (C1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All five G-quadruplex forming regions in the mitochondrial genome amplified between 10–18 cycles when qPCR was performed following BG4 pull-down.
source: Results showed that all five G-quadruplex forming regions amplified between 10–18 cycles when qPCR was performed (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Nine of 10 random regions did not show any amplification following the BG4 pull-down.
source: In contrast, 9 of 10 random regions did not show any amplification following the BG4 pull-down (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The control region (CR7) that amplified after BG4 pull-down had high GC content and a potential two-plate G4 DNA motif.
source: Sequence analysis showed that the control region (CR7) amplified after the BG4 pull-down had high GC content. Besides, when CR7 was analysed for potential non-B DNA formation, we noted the presence of two-plate G4 DNA motif.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and inference.

claim: CR7 may likely fold into a 2-plate G4 DNA, which could explain its binding with BG4.
source: CR7 may likely fold into a 2-plate G4 DNA, which could explain its binding with BG4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a speculation based on sequence analysis.

claim: Region I and other G4 motifs in the human mitochondrial genome could fold into G-quadruplex DNA.
source: Thus, our results suggest that Region I and other G4 motifs in the human mitochondrial genome could fold into G-quadruplex DNA.
evidence: This is based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Based on bisulphite DNA sequencing from Region I, the G4 structure may not be formed in all DNA molecules, and the frequency may be <25%.
source: However, based on bisulphite DNA sequencing from Region I, the structure may not be formed in all DNA molecules, and the frequency may be <25%.
evidence: This is inferred from the bisulphite sequencing data.

claim: Mitochondrial extract from rat tissues induces a concentration-dependent decrease in supercoiled form and increase in the nicked form of plasmid DNA containing mitochondrial Region I (pDI1).
source: Interestingly, a concentration-dependent decrease in supercoiled form and increase in the nicked form of plasmid DNA was observed when treated with mitochondrial extracts (Figure 6B, lanes 1–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was a concentration-dependent increase in the linear form of the plasmid DNA when treated with mitochondrial extract, indicating presence of two different nicks at proximity leading to a DSB.
source: Further, there was also a concentration-dependent increase in the linear form of the plasmid DNA, indicating presence of two different nicks at proximity leading to a DSB (Figure 6B, lanes 1–5, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C and inference from the results.

claim: There was a significant reduction in cleavage when two stretches of G's were mutated in the plasmid (pDI2).
source: Interestingly, there was a significant reduction in cleavage when two stretches of G's were mutated (Figure 6B, lanes 6–10, 6 C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), indicating the cleavage was indeed due to the presence of G4 DNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Primer extension studies revealed that mitochondrial extracts from both testes and spleen cleaved mitochondrial DNA at two specific nicking sites corresponding to the G-quadruplex forming region.
source: Results revealed two specific nicking sites when incubated with mitochondrial extracts from both testes and spleen. These were mapped to the position corresponding to the G-quadruplex forming region when the DNA sequencing ladder was used as a marker (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mutation of the G4 motif resulted in a significant reduction of cleavage activity, as one of the two cleavage sites disappeared when 2 G stretches were mutated (pDI2).
source: Interestingly, mutation of the G4 motif resulted in a significant reduction of cleavage activity, as one of the two cleavage sites disappeared when 2 G stretches were mutated (pDI2) from the G4 motif (Figure 6E and F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E, F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The upper cleavage site remains unchanged with the mutation in pDI2, possibly due to G4 structure formation in alternate conformations.
source: However, the upper cleavage site remains unchanged with the mutation. This may be due to G4 structure formation in alternate conformations, as Region I can fold into multiple forms (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Dahal et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and a citation.

claim: Generation of mutation in third stretch of guanines in addition to the above-described mutation (pDR4) resulted in remarkable reduction in the cleavage activity and led to disappearance of both the bands.
source: Interestingly, generation of mutation in third stretch of guanines in addition to the above-described mutation (pDR4) resulted in remarkable reduction in the cleavage activity and led to disappearance of both the bands (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endonuclease G was shown to bind preferentially to the guanine-rich strands by a previous study.
source: Among different mitochondrial endonucleases, Endonuclease G was shown to bind preferentially to the guanine-rich strands by a previous study (Ruiz-Carrillo and Renaud, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Specific cleavage at kinked DNA by Endonuclease G has been reported.
source: In a different study, specific cleavage at kinked DNA by Endonuclease G has also been reported (Ohsato et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Purified Endonuclease G showed a conformation change from supercoiled to open circular in the wild-type plasmid (pDI1) but not in the mutant plasmid (pDI2).
source: Results showed that while the wild-type plasmid (pDI1) showed a conformation change from supercoiled to open circular, mutant plasmid (pDI2) retained its supercoiled form (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The linear form of the plasmid DNA was observed when a higher concentration (60, 90, 120 ng) of Endonuclease G was used for the cleavage in the case of pDI1.
source: Besides, the linear form of the plasmid DNA was also observed when a higher concentration (60, 90, 120 ng) of Endonuclease G was used for the cleavage in the case of pDI1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Primer extension studies revealed that Endonuclease G cleaved mitochondrial DNA at multiple sites corresponding to a region of G-quadruplex DNA formation at Region I when it was present on pDI1.
source: Interestingly, primer extension studies revealed that Endonuclease G cleaved mitochondrial DNA at multiple sites corresponding to a region of G-quadruplex DNA formation at Region I when it was present on pDI1 (Figure 7C, lanes 1–3, 5–8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The primary two cleavage positions by Endonuclease G were comparable to the one observed when the mitochondrial extract was used for the study.
source: Importantly, the primary two cleavage positions were comparable to the one observed when the mitochondrial extract was used for the study (Figure 7C, lane 2–4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: When a protein with a mutation at the nuclease domain of Endonuclease G (ΔH151A) was used, the cleavage activity was abrogated.
source: More importantly, when a protein with a mutation at the nuclease domain of Endonuclease G (ΔH151A) was used, the cleavage activity was abrogated (Figure 7D and E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D, E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Endonucleases such as CtIP, FEN1 and RAGs did not exhibit any significant cleavage at Region I, unlike Endonuclease G.
source: Further, when endonucleases such as CtIP, FEN1 and RAGs were used for cleavage assay, results showed that, unlike Endonuclease G, none of the purified endonucleases exhibited any significant cleavage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1J), although the presence of CtIP (Tadi et al., 2016) and FEN1 (Kalifa et al., 2009; Klungland and Lindahl, 1997; Tadi et al., 2016) has been shown previously in mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1J and citations.

claim: Immunodepletion of Endonuclease G from mitochondrial extracts showed a significant reduction in cleavage efficiency at the mitochondrial G-quadruplex Region I.
source: Immunodepletion of Endonuclease G from mitochondrial extracts prepared from rat testes showed a significant reduction in cleavage efficiency at the mitochondrial G-quadruplex Region I, compared to beads alone control (Figure 7F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F–I.

claim: Immunodepletion of MGME1 from mitochondrial extracts did not result in any significant difference in the cleavage efficacy.
source: However, immunodepletion of MGME1, another important nuclease known to be present in mitochondria, did not result in any significant difference in the cleavage efficacy (Figure 7G–I; Phillips et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G–I and citations.

claim: The cleavage activity was restored when purified Endonuclease G was added back following its immunodepletion from the extract.
source: Importantly, the activity was restored when purified Endonuclease G was added back following its immunodepletion from the extract, confirming the role of Endonuclease G in the cleavage (Figure 7J and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7J and K.

claim: Endonuclease G localizes to mitochondria in HeLa, HEK 293T, and MEF cell lines.
source: Merge of MitoTracker with tagged Endonuclease G revealed localization of Endonuclease G in mitochondria in HeLa (human cervical cancer), HEK 293T (human embryonic kidney epithelial) and MEF (mouse embryonic fibroblast) cell lines (Figure 8A and B; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A, B, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endonuclease G colocalizes with TFAM, a transcription factor present in the mitochondrial matrix, indicating the presence of Endonuclease G in the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Results revealed low but distinct levels of colocalisation of Endonuclease G and TFAM, indicating the presence of Endonuclease G in the mitochondrial matrix (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of Endonuclease G in HeLa cells resulted in a significant reduction in cleavage efficiency at Region I.
source: Cleavage assay using mitochondrial extracts following knockdown of Endonuclease G revealed a significant reduction in cleavage efficiency at Region I, as that of scrambled control, suggesting its role in mitochondria in the context of cells (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: BG4 colocalizes with Endonuclease G in HeLa cells.
source: Yellow foci in the merged image suggested colocalisation of BG4 to Endonuclease G. Approximately 100 cells were analysed for colocalisation of anti-BG4 and anti-Endonuclease G using the Mander's colocalisation coefficient, for red over green, was ~0.32, while green over red was ~0.21 indicating the binding of Endonuclease G to G-quadruplex DNA structure (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9A and quantitative analysis in Figure 9B.

claim: Endonuclease G can bind to all G quadruplex regions (GR1-GR5) in the mitochondrial genome, while the control regions (CR1-CR10) did not bind to Endonuclease G.
source: The threshold values presented as a bar diagram suggested that Endonuclease G can bind to all G quadruplex regions (GR1- GR5), including the one present at mitochondrial Region I, while the control regions (CR1-CR10) (not known to form canonical G quadruplex) did not bind to Endonuclease G (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Endonuclease G binds to G-quadruplex regions of the mitochondrial genome when mitochondrial extract was incubated with mitochondrial DNA.
source: Further, the mitochondrial extract was incubated with the mitochondrial DNA, and a pull-down assay was done using Endonuclease G antibody (Figure 9C). Following the pull-down, beads were separated and loaded for protein analysis and western to confirm the pull-down (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A). The remaining was used for DNA isolation, followed by real-time and semiquantitative PCR. Results suggested the binding of Endonuclease G to G-quadruplex regions (Figure 9C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C–E and Figure 9—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Endonuclease G binding assay inside cells showed specific amplification of G quadruplex regions and no amplification of control regions.
source: Endonuclease G binding assay inside cells was performed to assess the binding of Endonuclease G to mitochondrial G4 DNA (Figure 9F, Figure 9—figure supplement 1C). The antibody-bound mitochondrial DNA was used for real-time PCR to amplify the G quadruplex regions and control regions. Results showed specific amplification of G quadruplex regions and no amplification of control regions, suggesting the specificity of Endonuclease G to G quadruplex regions within the cells (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Binding of Endonuclease G to G-rich strand (G1) partially rescued the sensitivity of P1 nuclease.
source: Interestingly, binding of Endonuclease G to G-rich strand (G1) partially rescued the sensitivity of P1 nuclease (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B, lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In the case of C-rich strands, mutants and random oligomers, protection from P1 nuclease by Endonuclease G was absent.
source: In contrast, in the case of C-rich strands, mutants and random oligomers, such protection was absent (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Exposure to Menadione, a mitochondria-specific ROS inducer, resulted in elevated levels of Endonuclease G in the mitochondrial matrix.
source: Results showed that exposure to stress conditions resulted in elevated levels of Endonuclease G in the matrix (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A and B.

claim: Under stress conditions, Endonuclease G may be released to the matrix from the inner membrane space where it binds to mitochondrial DNA and induces DNA breaks at Region I.
source: Based on the present and previous studies (García-Lepe and Bermúdez-Cruz, 2019; Tadi et al., 2016; Wisnovsky et al., 2018), we propose that under stress conditions, Endonuclease G may be released to the matrix from the inner membrane space where it binds to mitochondrial DNA. This could help the induce DNA breaks by Endonuclease G at Region I of the mitochondrial genome.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the current study and prior research.

claim: DNA modifying enzymes such as CtIP, MRN, and Exonuclease G may help in generating 3' overhangs following DNA breaks by Endonuclease G.
source: DNA modifying enzymes such as CtIP, MRN, and Exonuclease G may help in generating 3' overhangs, following which ligation of broken ends by an unknown mechanism leads to the '9 bp deletion' at the Region I of the mitochondrial genome (Figure 11).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 11.

claim: Ligation of broken ends by an unknown mechanism leads to the '9 bp deletion' at the Region I of the mitochondrial genome.
source: DNA modifying enzymes such as CtIP, MRN, and Exonuclease G may help in generating 3' overhangs, following which ligation of broken ends by an unknown mechanism leads to the '9 bp deletion' at the Region I of the mitochondrial genome (Figure 11).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 11.

claim: Five G-quadruplex DNA structures exist in the mitochondrial genome, all with three-plate conformation.
source: The present study in conjunction with previous studies, suggest the existence of five G-quadruplex DNA structures in the mitochondrial genome (Dahal et al., 2022; Damas et al., 2012; Dong et al., 2014), all with three-plate conformation that follows the general empirical formula for G-quadruplexes d(G3+N1-7G3+N1-7G3+N1-7G3+).
evidence: This is based on the current study and prior research.

claim: G-quadruplexes with three-plate are considered energetically stable.
source: G-quadruplexes with three-plate are considered energetically stable (Puig Lombardi and Londoño-Vallejo, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The presence of G-quadruplex motifs proximal to mitochondrial deletions has been reported.
source: The presence of G-quadruplex motifs proximal to mitochondrial deletions has been reported (Falabella et al., 2019a; Falabella et al., 2019b; Oliveira et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Computational analysis revealed that G4 sequences proximal to mtDNA deletions in several genetic diseases like Kearns-Sayre syndrome, Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome, Mitochondrial myopathy, Progressive external ophthalmoplegia.
source: Computational analysis (Bharti et al., 2014) revealed that G4 sequences proximal to mtDNA deletions in several genetic diseases like Kearns-Sayre syndrome, Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome, Mitochondrial myopathy, Progressive external ophthalmoplegia, etc.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The formation of intramolecular parallel G-quadruplex structure in the mitochondrial genome could make the region fragile due to increased probability of replication fork slippage or transcription arrest.
source: The formation of intramolecular parallel G-quadruplex structure in the mitochondrial genome could make the region fragile as there is an increased probability of replication fork slippage or transcription arrest at this region.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of G-quadruplex structures.

claim: RAGs can cleave at the G-quadruplex site in BCL2 MBR.
source: The action of RAGs at the G-quadruplex site in BCL2 MBR (Raghavan et al., 2004), MRE11 and DNA2 helicase on either side of the G-quadruplex structure in vitro (Masuda-Sasa et al., 2008) being some of the examples.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Endonuclease G has been reported to generate primers during mitochondrial DNA replication by DNA polymerase γ.
source: Previous studies have reported various other properties of Endonuclease G, which include the generation of primers during mitochondrial DNA replication by DNA polymerase γ, initiation of genomic inversion in herpes simplex type-1 virus (HSV-1), and its role during apoptosis (Côté et al., 1989; Parrish et al., 2001; Ruiz-Carrillo and Renaud, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Endonuclease G has been reported to initiate genomic inversion in herpes simplex type-1 virus (HSV-1).
source: Previous studies have reported various other properties of Endonuclease G, which include the generation of primers during mitochondrial DNA replication by DNA polymerase γ, initiation of genomic inversion in herpes simplex type-1 virus (HSV-1), and its role during apoptosis (Côté et al., 1989; Parrish et al., 2001; Ruiz-Carrillo and Renaud, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mammalian Endonuclease G is encoded in the nucleus.
source: Mammalian Endonuclease G is encoded in the nucleus (Gannavaram et al., 2008; Ohsato et al., 2002; Wiehe et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2016) and upon translocation to mitochondria, the mitochondrial targeting sequence is cleaved off such that a mature nuclease is released (Li et al., 2001; van Loo et al., 2001; Wiehe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Upon translocation to mitochondria, the mitochondrial targeting sequence of Endonuclease G is cleaved off such that a mature nuclease is released.
source: Mammalian Endonuclease G is encoded in the nucleus (Gannavaram et al., 2008; Ohsato et al., 2002; Wiehe et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2016) and upon translocation to mitochondria, the mitochondrial targeting sequence is cleaved off such that a mature nuclease is released (Li et al., 2001; van Loo et al., 2001; Wiehe et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: CPS-6, a mitochondrial endonuclease G in Caenorhabditis elegans, acts with maternal autophagy and proteasome machinery to promote paternal mitochondrial elimination.
source: CPS-6, a mitochondrial endonuclease G in Caenorhabditis elegans, acts with maternal autophagy and proteasome machinery to promote paternal mitochondrial elimination. It relocates from the intermembrane space of paternal mitochondria to the matrix after fertilisation to degrade mitochondrial DNA (Zhou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.
